title: Of idleness
paragraphs: Just as we see that pieces of ground long left idle and untilled, once they grow rich and fertile through rest, abound with and spend their virtue on producing countless kinds of weeds and wild herbs of no use — and that, to make them perform their proper office, we must cultivate and prepare them to receive seeds proper to our service; just as we see women who, without ever knowing a man, sometimes bring forth, of themselves, shapeless lumps of inanimate flesh, but who to bring about a natural and perfect generation must be served by another kind of seed — even so it is with minds, which, if not applied to some specific study to fix and restrain them, run riot in a thousand extravagances, drifting endlessly here and there in the vague expanse of imagination —
"Sicut aqua tremulum labris ubi lumen ahenis, Sole repercussum, aut radiantis imagine lunae, Omnia pervolitat late loca; jamque sub auras Erigitur, summique ferit laquearia tecti."

["As when in brazen vats of water the trembling light, reflected from the sun or from the image of the radiant moon, flits swiftly over every place around, and is now darted up on high to strike the panels of the ceiling overhead." — Aeneid, viii. 22.]
— and in this wild agitation there is no folly and no idle fancy they do not light upon:
["Like a sick man's dreams, creating empty phantoms." — Horace, Ars Poetica, 7.]
The soul that has no settled aim loses itself, for, as it is said —
["He who lives everywhere, lives nowhere." — Martial, vii. 73.]

When I lately retired to my own house, determined as far as I could to avoid any kind of involvement in affairs and to spend in privacy and peace the little time I have left to live, I imagined I could do my mind no greater favour than to leave it at full leisure to entertain and divert itself, and that I now hoped it might do so, being by this time more settled and more mature. But I find —
["Leisure always breeds shifting thoughts." — Lucan, iv. 704.]

— that, quite the contrary, it is like a horse that has broken from its rider and runs off into a much wilder career than any horseman would have urged on it, and it produces in me so many chimeras and fantastic monsters, one after another, without order or design, that, the better to contemplate at leisure their strangeness and absurdity, I have begun to set them down in writing, hoping in time to make my mind ashamed of itself.
